network.overall_strategy: This is an evidence-graded, conditional synthesis network, not ten experimentally established syntheses. The supplied literature cannot establish ten complete prebiotic routes to free cysteine or justify confidence of 0.9. The ten target-reaching sequences below comprise six variants of protected-cysteinyl synthesis, one provisional atmospheric-haze source, and three alternative recoveries from historically reported photochemical cystine. Foden et al. (2020) support the protected products, but their conversion to free cysteine remains unresolved. Accordingly, exhaustive acidic hydrolysis is explicitly represented as an unvalidated hypothesis, not as demonstrated neutral-water hydration and deprotection. The unsupported phosphate-precursor synthesis is omitted. Cystine recovery alternatives avoid that deprotection bottleneck but inherit the uncertainty of the historical cystine identification. All environments are anoxic and surface-associated; UV exposure is restricted to photochemical production, while subsequent processing requires shielding. No high-temperature hydrothermal synthesis or accumulation is claimed. Starting-reagent availability, separation between incompatible stages, product survival, and yields remain conditional. Equations in mechanism fields supply stoichiometric bookkeeping without repeating molecule IDs. Neutral molecular skeletons are used for organic compounds; their pH-dependent protonation is not separately enumerated. Atmospheric equations are bookkeeping closures, not experimentally established overall reactions.

reactions.name: Strecker formation of serine nitrile

conditions.other: Concentrated ammoniacal cyanide solution; anoxic and UV-shielded. Exact concentrations and reaction time must be taken from the primary experimental protocol rather than inferred from the supplied summary.

reactions.mechanism: Glycolaldehyde forms an imine with ammonia, followed by cyanide addition. Net: mol_001 + mol_002 + mol_003 -> mol_006 + mol_004.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED TRANSFORMATION: Foden et al. (2020) describe serine nitrile as a stable Strecker product obtained in greater than 90% yield with ammonium cyanide. Patel et al. (2015) support a possible upstream photochemical source of glycolaldehyde, but that multistep source is not collapsed into an invented elementary reaction here. Glycolaldehyde and concentrated cyanide are explicit boundary feedstocks. Residual aldehydes and cyanide must not accompany eventual free cysteine into a common reaction mixture.

reactions.name: Oxidatively activated N,O-diacetylation using thioacetic acid
agents: Ferricyanide, mol_008: consumed oxidant, not a catalyst

conditions.other: Near-neutral water; approximately 1 h in the reported laboratory acylation. Separate from free sulfide and abundant dissolved Fe2+. Before sulfur installation, residual ferricyanide must be removed or quantitatively consumed and its absence verified; simple sedimentation is not assumed to remove dissolved oxidant.

reactions.mechanism: Oxidative activation of thioacetic acid enables acetyl transfer to the amino and hydroxyl groups. Balanced net closure: 4 mol_006 + 8 mol_007 + 16 mol_008 -> 4 mol_012 + 16 mol_009 + 16 mol_010 + mol_011. S8 represents elemental-sulfur bookkeeping, not a claim that it is the sole measured sulfur coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED ORGANIC TRANSFORMATION: Foden et al. (2020) report up to 91% N,O-diacetylation. Ferricyanide is a stoichiometric oxidant and is therefore represented as a reactant. Its localized availability in an anoxic, generally reducing setting is unresolved. The published laboratory transformation does not establish a natural purification mechanism separating product from oxidant, iron-cyanide complexes, and excess reagents. This branch remains conditional on that separation; no mineral filtration efficiency is invented.

reactions.name: N,O-diacetylation using N-acetylimidazole

conditions.other: Neutral aqueous solution; staged addition of acetyl donor. Residual acetylating reagent must be depleted or removed before exposing the product to sulfide.

reactions.mechanism: Two nucleophilic acyl substitutions transfer acetyl groups to nitrogen and oxygen. Net: mol_006 + 2 mol_013 -> mol_012 + 2 mol_014.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED TRANSFORMATION: Foden et al. (2020) report N-acetylimidazole as an effective alternative acetylating reagent in neutral water. This route avoids ferricyanide-sulfide incompatibility, but it does not solve the prebiotic origin, concentration, or delivery of N-acetylimidazole. It is supplied explicitly rather than assigned an unsupported synthesis.

reactions.name: Nitrile-assisted acetate elimination

conditions.other: pH approximately 8; approximately 4 days; anoxic, UV-shielded solution. No Mg2+ requirement is assigned to this acetate-leaving-group route.

reactions.mechanism: General-base-assisted alpha deprotonation followed by beta elimination of acetate forms the activated alkene. N-acetylation stabilizes the dehydroalanine nitrile. Neutral-skeleton net: mol_012 -> mol_015 + mol_016.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED AND RATE-LIMITING UPSTREAM STEP: Foden et al. (2020) report approximately 85% conversion after four days near room temperature, with an optimum near pH 8. The nitrile is mechanistically important; the amide analogue does not justify the same elimination. The phosphate route is excluded because its precursor supply is unresolved and its Mg2+-enhanced conditions are incompletely specified in the supplied account.

reactions.name: Sulfide addition and nitrile thioamidation

conditions.temperature: 300-333 K; near-ambient conditions preferred for preservation
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm in an anoxic vessel or retained-sulfide water body
conditions.other: Near-neutral pH; sufficient dissolved sulfide for both alkene addition and nitrile conversion. Exact dose and duration are not specified by the supplied summary. Exclude residual ferricyanide and direct UV.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide adds to the beta carbon of the activated alkene; a further sulfide equivalent converts the nitrile into a thioamide. Net: mol_015 + 2 mol_005 -> mol_017.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED PROTECTED ENDPOINT: Foden et al. (2020) report near-quantitative formation of N-acetylcysteine thioamide. This is not free cysteine and not a cysteine carboxylate. No mineral catalyst is required. The reported conversion must not be multiplied into an overall free-cysteine yield because rxn_010 is unvalidated.

reactions.name: Thioacetic-acid conjugate addition

conditions.other: pH approximately 7; approximately 12 h; anoxic and UV-shielded.

reactions.mechanism: Thioacetate adds to the activated alkene, installing the beta sulfur atom as an S-acetyl thioester while retaining the nitrile. Net: mol_015 + mol_007 -> mol_018.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED TRANSFORMATION: Foden et al. (2020) report quantitative thioester formation over approximately 12 h at pH 7. The reaction provides a chemically justified alternative to direct sulfide addition and permits subsequent choice of ammonolysis or sulfidolysis. Thioacetic-acid availability remains a boundary assumption.

reactions.name: Selective S-deacetylation by ammonolysis

conditions.temperature: 300-333 K; candidate surface window, not a reconstructed experimental optimum
conditions.other: Ammoniacal aqueous workup. The supplied summary does not specify the exact ammonia concentration, pH, or duration; those values require the primary protocol. Avoid prolonged strongly alkaline exposure.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia attacks the thioester carbonyl, releasing the side-chain thiol and producing acetamide. The N-acetyl group and nitrile remain intact. Net: mol_018 + mol_003 -> mol_019 + mol_020.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED PROTECTED ENDPOINT: Foden et al. (2020) report N-acetylcysteine nitrile in 77% yield following ammonolysis. This selective thioester cleavage is not N-deacetylation and does not generate the carboxyl group. It therefore supports formation of mol_019, not the proposed completion in rxn_009.

reactions.name: Sulfidolysis and thioamide formation

conditions.other: Near-neutral, anoxic aqueous sulfide workup. Exact reagent loading and duration must be recovered from the primary protocol rather than inferred from the reported yield.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide cleaves the S-acetyl thioester, and additional sulfide converts the retained nitrile to a thioamide. Net: mol_018 + 2 mol_005 -> mol_017 + mol_007.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED PROTECTED ENDPOINT: Foden et al. (2020) report approximately 95% formation of N-acetylcysteine thioamide by the thiolysis branch. The two sulfide equivalents in the net equation account for thioester cleavage and nitrile thioamidation. This does not demonstrate subsequent conversion to free cysteine.

reactions.name: Hypothetical exhaustive acidic hydrolysis of N-acetylcysteine nitrile
agents: Hydronium: proposed acid catalyst from a separate acidic reservoir

conditions.temperature: 350-370 K; proposed screening window, not a demonstrated operating condition
conditions.other: Proposed pH 0-1 in an anoxic, UV-shielded acidic water body; residence time and conversion are unknown. Feed must be separated from other nitriles, aldehydes, and oxidants. Cool promptly if cysteine is detected. Availability of sufficiently acidic water and adequate reaction selectivity are unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized acid-catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis through an amide, followed by hydrolysis of the N-acetyl bond. Net neutral-skeleton equation: mol_019 + 3 mol_004 -> mol_021 + mol_016 + mol_003. Ammonia and the amino group would be protonated in the acidic reaction medium.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE COMPLETION AND MAJOR BOTTLENECK: Foden et al. (2020) do not demonstrate this sequence. Acid catalysis is chemically more defensible than asserting rapid, uncatalyzed neutral-water hydrolysis, but no substrate-specific rates, yields, or thiol-compatible deprotection protocol are supplied. Combining the hydrolyses into one net node does not close the experimental gap. Rossetto et al. (2022) establish thermal vulnerability of cysteine-containing peptides, not a survival rate for free cysteine under these acidic conditions. This edge cannot support a quantified complete synthesis until product-selective time-course experiments establish that hydrolysis outruns degradation.

reactions.name: Hypothetical hydrolytic conversion of N-acetylcysteine thioamide to cysteine
agents: Hydronium: proposed acid catalyst from a separate acidic reservoir

conditions.temperature: 350-370 K; proposed screening window, not demonstrated
conditions.other: Proposed pH 0-1; anoxic, UV-shielded and isolated from residual oxidants. No validated residence time is available. Sulfide loss, thiol preservation, thioamide hydrolysis and N-deacetylation must all be measured independently.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized hydrolysis of the thioamide carbon to a carboxyl group, releasing ammonia and sulfide, together with N-deacetylation. Net neutral-skeleton equation: mol_017 + 3 mol_004 -> mol_021 + mol_016 + mol_003 + mol_005. This net node does not assert an experimentally resolved order of individual hydrolyses.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE COMPLETION AND MAJOR BOTTLENECK: The supported endpoint in Foden et al. (2020) is mol_017. The supplied evidence establishes neither selective hydrolytic sulfur removal nor the subsequent release of free cysteine. No oxidant or unreported mineral catalyst is inserted to make the conversion appear established. Rossetto et al. (2022) justify caution about heating but do not validate this proposed acidic window. A positive result requires cysteine-specific identification, material balance, and survival controls; simply supplying water does not establish an adequate rate.

reactions.name: Empirical atmospheric-haze source of cysteine

conditions.other: Far-UV irradiation of N2 containing approximately 0.1% CH4, 0.5% CO2 and 5 ppmv H2S. No molecular oxygen. Any subsequent collection must preserve anoxia and avoid prolonged UV irradiation; survival after natural deposition is unestablished.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved radical and aerosol chemistry. Atom-balanced source-term closure: mol_024 + 4 mol_022 + 2 mol_023 + 2 mol_005 -> 2 mol_021 + 3 mol_025. This equation is not a measured exclusive conversion; hydrogen is a bookkeeping coproduct, not an asserted analytical observation. No speculative ethanethiol-to-cysteamine-to-cysteine sequence is promoted to established elementary reactions.
reactions.reasoning: PROVISIONAL DIRECT-TARGET EVIDENCE: Reed et al. (2025) report high-resolution mass-spectral, fragmentation, isotope and control evidence consistent with cysteine in photochemical haze. This is stronger evidence for the actual free-cysteine target than inference from protected derivatives. However, isolated yield, quantitative production rate, independent replication, exact mechanism and environmental accumulation remain unresolved. The planetary flux estimate is not used as a reaction yield or an accumulation measurement.

reactions.name: Historically reported UV production of cystine

conditions.temperature: Approximately 300 K; network assignment rather than a reconstructed experimental value
conditions.other: UV irradiation of a reducing CH4/NH3/H2S mixture with water vapor or water contact. H2S absorbs the incident radiation. Exact spectrum, gas ratios and exposure time must be taken from the original experiments. Oxygen-free collection is essential to distinguish reactor formation from workup oxidation.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved photochemical sulfur-organic synthesis and possible radical disulfide formation. Atom-balanced bookkeeping closure: 6 mol_022 + 2 mol_003 + 2 mol_005 + 4 mol_004 -> mol_026 + 15 mol_025. Neither the exclusive product distribution nor hydrogen production is established by this equation.
reactions.reasoning: LOW-CONFIDENCE HISTORICAL SOURCE: Khare and Sagan (1971) reported cystine from UV experiments involving H2S. The identification predates modern structural analysis and has not been independently confirmed with contemporary methods. Anoxic disulfide formation is chemically possible through radical chemistry, but the supplied evidence does not exclude oxidation during collection or analysis. Consequently, this edge is retained only as a conditional source; it is not upgraded using Parker et al. (2011), whose reanalysis did not establish cysteine production.

reactions.name: Hypothetical native-iron reduction of cystine
agents: Native iron, mol_027: consumed electron donor, not a catalyst

conditions.other: Proposed mildly acidic water, pH 4-6; anoxic and UV-shielded. Contact with fresh Fe0 followed by separation from the metal surface. No heating or drying of cysteine with the resulting Fe2+ is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Two-electron disulfide reduction coupled to Fe0 oxidation. Net: mol_026 + mol_027 + 2 mol_010 -> 2 mol_021 + mol_028.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE PREBIOTIC APPLICATION: Conventional disulfide redox chemistry motivates Fe0 as an electron donor, but no supplied study demonstrates this cystine-to-cysteine reaction under the proposed conditions. Kitadai et al. (2019) establish other reductive transformations involving reduced iron materials, not cystine reduction or cysteine synthesis. Surface passivation, competing hydrogen evolution, metal-thiolate binding and desulfurization could suppress recoverable free cysteine. This pathway also depends on confirming the historical cystine source of Khare and Sagan (1971).

reactions.name: Hypothetical sulfide-mediated recovery of cysteine from cystine

conditions.other: Proposed pH 7-8; anoxic and UV-shielded. Sulfide loading, residence time and sulfur partitioning require measurement. Formation of cysteine persulfide and soluble polysulfides must be monitored rather than treated as quantitative cysteine production.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed sulfur exchange begins with sulfide attack on the disulfide and formation of thiolate/persulfide intermediates. A possible overall redox closure is 8 mol_026 + 8 mol_005 -> 16 mol_021 + mol_011. The equation does not establish that the sulfur-exchange network reaches this endpoint.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE: No supplied paper demonstrates complete sulfide reduction of photochemical cystine to free cysteine. The chemical motivation is nucleophilic sulfur exchange with a geochemically available reagent, but persulfidation and polysulfide equilibria may prevent the proposed endpoint. Khare and Sagan (1971) support only the uncertain upstream cystine report. This is a distinct testable recovery hypothesis, not another validated origin of the cysteine carbon skeleton.

reactions.name: Proposed cystine sulfitolysis releasing one cysteine equivalent

conditions.other: Proposed pH 7-8.5 with excess sulfite; anoxic and UV-shielded. Sulfite is a simple boundary reagent potentially supplied by dissolution and neutralization of volcanic SO2. Its local concentration and compatibility with other pool constituents remain unspecified.

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic sulfite attack cleaves the disulfide, producing cysteine thiolate and an S-sulfonated cysteinyl product; proton transfer gives the encoded cysteine skeleton. Net: mol_026 + mol_029 + mol_010 -> mol_021 + mol_030.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE PREBIOTIC DEPLOYMENT OF GENERAL SULFITOLYSIS CHEMISTRY: The supplied research contains no direct demonstration of this recovery step. Its chemical merit is disulfide cleavage without molecular oxygen, high temperatures or N-deacetylation. One cysteine residue remains trapped as S-sulfocysteine, so this equation releases only one free-cysteine equivalent per cystine molecule; no unreported recovery of the second residue is assumed. Reaction extent and product survival need verification, and the upstream source remains the low-confidence report of Khare and Sagan (1971).

pathways.name: Oxidative acetylation followed by direct sulfide addition
pathways.description: Supported synthesis reaches N-acetylcysteine thioamide. Free cysteine is reached only through the unvalidated acidic hydrolysis hypothesis in rxn_010. Ferricyanide separation is an additional geochemical bottleneck.

pathways.name: Oxidative acetylation followed by thioacetate addition and ammonolysis
pathways.description: Supported transformations furnish N-acetylcysteine nitrile through selective S-deacetylation. The terminal nitrile hydrolysis and N-deacetylation represented by rxn_009 remain unvalidated.

pathways.name: Oxidative acetylation followed by thioacetate addition and sulfidolysis
pathways.description: An experimentally supported alternative sulfur-installation sequence converges on N-acetylcysteine thioamide. It does not resolve the shared rxn_010 free-cysteine bottleneck.

pathways.name: Acetylimidazole activation followed by direct sulfide addition
pathways.description: Avoids ferricyanide during activation and reaches the supported protected thioamide. Acetylimidazole availability and the unvalidated completion in rxn_010 remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Acetylimidazole activation followed by thioacetate addition and ammonolysis
pathways.description: An oxidant-free activation variant leading to N-acetylcysteine nitrile. Formation of free cysteine remains conditional on demonstrating rxn_009 with adequate thiol preservation.

pathways.name: Acetylimidazole activation followed by thioacetate addition and sulfidolysis
pathways.description: Combines the supported non-ferricyanide activation and sulfidolysis branches. Its protected endpoint is experimentally supported, but its free-cysteine endpoint depends on rxn_010.

pathways.name: Direct atmospheric-haze source
pathways.description: Reed et al. (2025) provide provisional analytical evidence for cysteine itself. This empirical source has no resolved intermediate sequence, isolated yield, demonstrated deposition survival or independent replication.

pathways.name: Historical photochemical cystine followed by native-iron reduction
pathways.description: Combines a low-confidence historical cystine source with a proposed Fe0-driven disulfide reduction. Both confirmation of the source and selective recovery of free cysteine are required.

pathways.name: Historical photochemical cystine followed by sulfide-mediated recovery
pathways.description: Tests whether sulfur exchange with sulfide can release cysteine from the historically reported cystine. Persulfide and polysulfide trapping may block completion. This is not a demonstrated synthesis.

pathways.name: Historical photochemical cystine followed by sulfitolysis
pathways.description: Uses a chemically distinct disulfide-cleavage hypothesis to release one cysteine equivalent while retaining the other residue as S-sulfocysteine. Prebiotic implementation and the historical upstream identification remain unvalidated.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Foden et al. (2020) support the sequence through N-acetylcysteine thioamide, not the final production of free cysteine. rxn_010 is balanced but lacks demonstrated conditions for complete thioamide hydrolysis and N-deacetylation with acceptable cysteine recovery. rxn_002 is experimentally supported, but residual ferricyanide must be controlled before sulfide addition and thiol accumulation. The narrative acknowledges this separation without establishing its physical implementation.
suggestions: Specify reaction-specific concentrations, pH, temperature and duration, including the approximately four-day, pH-8 elimination supported by Foden et al.
Demonstrate oxidant removal or consumption before sulfur addition, then measure free-cysteine yield and sulfur-containing byproducts during the proposed acidic hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The thioacetate-addition and selective ammonolysis sequence agrees with Foden et al. (2020), including formation of N-acetylcysteine nitrile rather than free cysteine. rxn_009 correctly includes enough water for nitrile hydrolysis and deacetylation, but stoichiometry does not establish selective conversion or product survival. Oxidant carryover and the transition from ammonolysis to acidic processing remain operational gaps.
suggestions: Determine whether nitrile hydrolysis can precede N-deacetylation, and monitor possible aminothiol reactions with residual nitriles during processing and neutralization.
Specify ferricyanide removal, ammonia concentration, acid addition and intermediate recovery; report isolated or independently quantified free cysteine rather than disappearance of starting material.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Foden et al. (2020) support the protected-product chemistry, including conversion through the thioacetate adduct to N-acetylcysteine thioamide. rxn_008 is balanceable with two sulfide equivalents and does not remove the N-acetyl group. Consequently, this sequence still depends on the unvalidated rxn_010. Its additional sulfur-transfer chemistry does not itself establish free-cysteine release.
suggestions: Record sulfide loading, pH and residence time for rxn_008, and verify the thioamide product in the actual preceding reaction mixture.
Test rxn_010 with explicit acid conditions and quantify cysteine, partially hydrolyzed intermediates, sulfur loss and decomposition products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: N-acetylimidazole-mediated activation is supported by Foden et al. (2020) and avoids the specific ferricyanide-carryover problem. Its effective concentration and competition with aqueous hydrolysis still require specification. The pathway reaches a supported protected cysteinyl product, but rxn_010 remains experimentally unvalidated. This is an evidence gap, not proof that acidic hydrolysis and deacetylation are chemically impossible.
suggestions: Specify acetylating-agent equivalents, dosing and reaction conditions sufficient for both N- and O-acetylation in the proposed mixture.
Establish a hydrolysis/deprotection operating window experimentally; do not extrapolate cysteine survival from anoxia alone or from unrelated high-temperature peptide measurements.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The protected synthesis and S-deacetylation chemistry align with Foden et al. (2020). Ammonolysis produces N-acetylcysteine nitrile; it does not achieve the target. rxn_009 must subsequently hydrolyze the nitrile and remove N-acetyl protection while retaining the thiol. Neither the necessary operating conditions nor an experimentally supported free-cysteine yield is supplied.
suggestions: Resolve rxn_009 into observable hydrolysis and deacetylation stages, including any N-acetylcysteine amide or acid intermediates actually detected.
Validate the sequence without assuming purified intermediates, or explicitly describe separation operations and their recovery efficiencies.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The acetylimidazole, elimination, thioacetate-addition and sulfidolysis sequence is consistent with the protected-product chemistry reported by Foden et al. (2020). The identified thioamide is not free cysteine, so target achievement remains conditional on rxn_010. The generic Surface designation and shielding requirement do not specify the acidity, temperature or duration needed for that conversion.
suggestions: Measure hydrolysis and N-deacetylation rates separately, alongside cysteine survival under the same conditions.
Specify the transition from sulfide-rich synthesis to acidic processing, including sulfide volatilization, retained sulfur species and product recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This has the strongest direct evidence for the requested free-cysteine target. Reed et al. (2025) provide exact-mass, fragmentation, isotope and control evidence, which is substantially stronger than a formula-only assignment. Nevertheless, the source remains unquantified and independently unreplicated in the supplied literature. rxn_011 is acceptable as a bookkeeping source term, not as an experimentally established overall stoichiometry or mechanism. Deposition and subsequent survival remain unresolved.
suggestions: Specify the gas mixture, irradiation spectrum, photon flux and production location, including whether the experimental far-UV wavelengths are available there.
Replicate identification using authentic standards and orthogonal thiol-sensitive analysis, quantify cysteine yield, and measure recovery after deposition into shielded anoxic water.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Khare and Sagan's historical cystine report provides limited upstream evidence because modern confirmation is absent. Iron-mediated disulfide reduction is thermodynamically plausible, but selective recovery in this mixture is unvalidated; proton corrosion, sulfur-induced surface passivation and product binding could compete. The mol_028 formula/InChI discrepancy also requires correction. The supplied audit nevertheless classifies rxn_013 as balanceable, so it is not a reported conservation violation.
suggestions: Confirm photochemical cystine with modern chromatography, standards and sulfur-sensitive analysis before evaluating downstream recovery.
Define reactive iron availability and surface condition, then measure cysteine recovery against corrosion, passivation and adsorption.
Reconcile mol_028's formula and InChI using an unambiguous single Fe atom with charge +2, such as [Fe+2], and rerun the representation audit.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway combines the uncertain historical cystine source with an unresolved sulfur-speciation step. Sulfide attack on disulfides can produce a thiol and a persulfide; that does not establish clean conversion to two cysteine equivalents plus elemental sulfur. rxn_014 conserves atoms and charge under the supplied audit, but its proposed endpoint requires evidence distinguishing cysteine from persulfides and polysulfides.
suggestions: Reproduce and quantify the cystine source using modern analytical methods.
Measure pH-dependent sulfur speciation and cysteine yield during sulfide treatment; represent persulfide or polysulfide intermediates if observed rather than assuming an S8 endpoint.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Sulfitolysis is a chemically credible disulfide-cleavage reaction, and rxn_015 correctly releases one cysteine equivalent while retaining the other cysteinyl unit as S-sulfocysteine. It does not require an additional conversion of that coproduct to satisfy the stated target. However, the complete pathway still depends on the uncertain historical cystine identification. Sulfite concentration, pH-dependent nucleophilicity, cystine solubility and recovery are unspecified.
suggestions: Confirm and quantify the photochemical cystine precursor independently.
Specify and test sulfitolysis pH, sulfite loading and residence time, measuring free cysteine separately from S-sulfocysteine and accounting for the one-equivalent recovery limit.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally strong: its 30 molecule nodes and 15 reaction nodes form a connected graph, and the supplied deterministic audit reports no atom/charge conservation violations. The coefficients involving S8 are ordinary stoichiometric scaling, not evidence of implausible molecularity. The mol_028 formula/InChI inconsistency should be corrected without reclassifying rxn_013 as unbalanced. Literature alignment is strong in distinguishing protected cysteinyl products from free cysteine and explicitly labeling unsupported endpoints. Nevertheless, citations and operating conditions should be attached to individual reaction records rather than left largely at strategy level. The decisive limitation is completion of target-forming chemistry: P1-P6 lack validated hydrolysis/deprotection to free cysteine; P8-P10 depend on an inadequately confirmed cystine source; and P7 provides meaningful modern evidence but no established yield, deposition recovery or accumulation. Anoxia and shielding are sensible safeguards, but physical transfers, oxidant removal, reaction-specific conditions and product survival remain conditional. The hypothetical labels improve evidentiary honesty but do not validate those transformations. Overall confidence reflects these network-level completion and compatibility gaps, not pathway counts, shared molecules, or preference for any feedstock or framework. The network is a useful conditional research plan, but it is not APPROVED at the required 0.90 threshold.
